title: Machine Learning Examples
description: Small Machine Learning examples from the lessons. Each example links back to its explanation and practice task.

examples.title: Learn from examples
examples.description: Machine learning uses examples to choose a rule or model. A model is a stored way to make predictions. A prediction is an estimate, not a known fact.

examples.title: Inputs and known answers
examples.description: A feature is an input used for a prediction. A label is the known answer in a teaching example. Keep each input paired with the right answer.

examples.title: Regression predicts numbers
examples.description: Regression is a task that predicts a number. Here we supply a doubling rule ourselves so the calculation is easy to inspect.

examples.title: Classification chooses a group
examples.description: Classification predicts a group label. For this toy example, a threshold is the number where our choice changes.

examples.title: Try the nearest example
examples.description: A nearest-neighbour rule uses the closest stored example. Distance tells us how far two values are apart. Here distance is the size of their difference.
examples.code:
examples = [(1, "small"), (3, "small"), (8, "large")]
query = 7
nearest = min(examples, key=lambda row: abs(row[0] - query))
print(nearest[1])

examples.title: Keep a test set aside
examples.description: Training examples help choose a model. Test examples are kept aside to check it later. Keeping them separate helps reveal mistakes on unseen data.
examples.code:
rows = [(1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8)]
train = rows[:3]
test = rows[3:]
print(len(train), len(test))

examples.title: Compare with a baseline
examples.description: A baseline is a simple prediction rule used for comparison. Always guessing the training average is one baseline for a number task.

examples.title: Measure a numeric mistake
examples.description: Absolute error is the size of the difference between an answer and a prediction. It drops the minus sign so the size is always nonnegative.
examples.code:
answers = [4, 8]
predictions = [5, 6]
errors = [abs(a - p) for a, p in zip(answers, predictions)]
print(errors, sum(errors) / len(errors))

examples.title: Accuracy needs context
examples.description: Accuracy is the share of group guesses that are correct. It can hide poor performance on a rare group.
examples.code:
answers = ["dry", "dry", "dry", "rain"]
predictions = ["dry"] * 4
correct = sum(a == p for a, p in zip(answers, predictions))
print(correct / len(answers))

examples.title: Memorising is not generalising
examples.description: Overfitting happens when a model follows training details too closely and does poorly on new examples. Generalising means working on useful new cases.

examples.title: Group without answer labels
examples.description: Clustering groups similar inputs without known class labels. Here we check distance to two fixed centres; a real clustering method can learn its centres.
examples.code:
centres = [2, 8]
point = 7
distances = [abs(point - centre) for centre in centres]
print(distances.index(min(distances)))

examples.title: Write an honest model report
examples.description: A useful model report explains the task, data, checks and limits. Readers need enough detail to know where the result may fail.
examples.code:
Task: estimate reading minutes
Data: fictional page-and-time pairs
Check: compare held-out errors with a simple baseline
Limit: too little data for real learners
Decision: keep this as a classroom demonstration
